extra.message: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 from_string

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The `username` query parameter is accepted directly from the HTTP query string via FastAPI route handler `read_root(username=None)` at line 8. The user-supplied string is concatenated into a Jinja2 template string on line 14 via `from_string("Welcome " + username + "!").render()`. Because Jinja2 evaluates template expressions ({{...}}, {%...%}) at render time and `Environment()` is created without any sandboxing, an attacker can inject arbitrary template syntax. SINK: The rendered output is returned via `HTMLResponse(content=output)` at line 19, confirming the result. An attacker can achieve RCE by injecting e.g. `{{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read() }}`, demonstrating code execution on the server. The commented-out safe implementation on line 17 shows the developer was aware of the correct pattern (passing user input as a template variable) but left the vulnerable code active.

SOURCE: The `username` query parameter (line 8) is untrusted user input. It flows through `Jinja2.from_string(...).render()` (line 14) where Jinja2's default `Environment()` has `autoescape=False` (see line 11), so HTML in the input passes through unescaped. SINK: The resulting string is passed to `HTMLResponse(content=output)` (line 19), which serves it as `text/html` without Content-Type sanitization or CSP headers. An attacker visiting `/?username=` will have the script rendered and executed in the victim's browser. The `autoescape=False` default is confirmed at line 11 where `Environment()` is created without the `autoescape=True` argument.

extra.message: Missing security headers on HTML response (CSP / X-Frame-Options / X-Content-Type-Options)

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The HTMLResponse at line 19 does not set any security headers: no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, nor X-Content-Type-Options. SINK: The browser receives the response with default security policies only. An attacker can embed this page in an iframe (clickjacking), the browser may MIME-sniff the response differently, and the reflected XSS (already identified at line 19) has no CSP to mitigate it. FastAPI/Starlette supports adding headers via the `headers` parameter or middleware, but none are configured.

extra.message: Unpinned third-party dependencies allow supply-chain compromise

metadata.proof: SOURCE: All three dependencies (fastapi, uvicorn, jinja2) are specified without version pinning in requirements.txt. SINK: Running `pip install -r requirements.txt` will install the latest available versions, which could silently introduce malicious code or breaking changes. An attacker who compromises the PyPI package for any of these dependencies, or a dependency of a dependency, can distribute a tainted version that will be auto-installed on next deployment. Pinning to known-good versions with hash verification (e.g. `fastapi==0.78.0 --hash=sha256:...`) is the standard mitigation.

extra.message: Jinja2 Environment created without autoescape=True — HTML output not escaped

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The Jinja2 `Environment()` is created at line 11 without `autoescape=True`. Jinja2's default `select_autoescape()` infers autoescape from the template file extension, but `from_string()` templates have no filename, so autoescape silently defaults to `False`. SINK: Any user-supplied value containing `<script>`, `'`, `"`, `<`, `>`, or `&` is rendered verbatim into the HTML response at line 19. This means even the safe implementation (commented-out line 17: `{{ user_name }}`) would NOT escape HTML entities in `username`, enabling XSS independently of the SSTI flaw. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the `username` parameter, e.g. `/?username=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`.
